titre: The Corwin Amendment (1861): The First 13th Amendment Protected Slavery
accroche: On March 2, 1861, the U.S. Congress adopts an amendment that guarantees slavery in the states. It would have been the thirteenth; the number will go to abolition.
contenu_vulgarise:
On March 4, 1861, in his inaugural address, Abraham Lincoln mentions an amendment whose text he says he has not seen. He has understood, he says, that it was passed by Congress and that it provides that the federal government will never interfere with the “domestic institutions” of the states, including that of “persons held to service.” Holding this rule to be already implicit in constitutional law, he has, he declares, “no objection to its being made express and irrevocable.” This amendment would have been the thirteenth of the United States Constitution.

## A Text That Forbids Amending

On February 26, 1861, Representative Thomas Corwin of Ohio introduces the text, in a secession crisis in which Congress is trying to hold on to the South. It creates no right: it forbids certain future revisions. “No amendment shall be made to the Constitution which will authorize or give to Congress the power to abolish or interfere, within any State, with the domestic institutions thereof, including that of persons held to labor or service by the laws of said State.” In other words, it places slavery, where it exists, beyond the reach of any revision that would give Congress the power over it.

The House adopts it on February 28, 1861, by 133 votes to 65, just above the two-thirds required. The Senate adopts it on March 2 by 24 votes to 12, exactly two-thirds. The outgoing president, James Buchanan, signs it, which is not necessary: the amendment procedure gives him no role. Lincoln, once in office, sends it to the states for ratification, according to the U.S. National Archives.

## A Number That Changes Meaning

The text does not hold the South. By summer 1861, eleven Southern states have seceded, and four years of civil war follow. The amendment never gathers three-quarters of the states and does not enter the Constitution.

On January 31, 1865, Congress adopts another text, which says the opposite: “Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction.” On December 6, 1865, Georgia becomes the twenty-seventh state to ratify it, which crosses the three-quarters threshold. Secretary of State William Seward certifies the adoption on December 18. It is this text that bears the number XIII.

## What This Changes

The Thirteenth Amendment is read as the natural endpoint of a country moving away from slavery. The National Archives recall that, four years earlier, Congress voted for the opposite text, to appease the South. What the Constitution retains from a proposal does not depend on the majority that votes for it, but on the three-quarters of the states that ratify it: it is that ratification that made the number XIII the abolition, and not the guarantee.

What is a guarantee worth when declared “irrevocable,” if those it is meant for have already begun to leave?

repere.texte: On February 28, 1861, the U.S. House adopts the Corwin Amendment by 133 votes to 65, and the Senate adopts it on March 2 by 24 votes to 12, exactly two-thirds. It forbids any amendment giving Congress the power to abolish slavery in the states or to interfere with it.
repere.source: National Archives (United States), “Unratified Amendments: Protection of Slavery,” February 19, 2020

carte.punch: The number XIII almost protected slavery: Congress voted for it on March 2, 1861.
carte.idee: On March 2, 1861, the U.S. Senate adopts, by exactly two-thirds, the Corwin Amendment: no future amendment could give Congress the power to abolish slavery in the states. It never gathers three-quarters of the states. The number XIII will go to the 1865 abolition.

quiz.question: What did the Corwin Amendment, adopted by the U.S. Congress on March 2, 1861, provide?
choix: That slavery would be abolished in stages in the Northern states only
That no amendment could give Congress the power to abolish slavery in the states
That Congress would buy from Southern owners the people held in slavery
That states could leave the Union after a vote of their legislature
quiz.explication: The text introduced by Corwin forbids any amendment that would authorize Congress to abolish slavery in a state or to interfere with its domestic institutions. It provides for neither partial abolition, nor buyout, nor a right of secession. It never gathers three-quarters of the states, and the number XIII will go in 1865 to the opposite text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did President Buchanan's signature on the Corwin Amendment have no legal effect?
choix: Because the constitutional amendment procedure gives the president no role
Because Buchanan had left office before signing
Because Congress had already withdrawn the text by the time of the signature
Because only the Senate can validly sign an amendment
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The U.S. constitutional amendment procedure gives the president no role: Buchanan's signature, though real, was not necessary and changed nothing about the fate of the text.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What makes the number XIII that of the abolition of slavery, rather than that of the Corwin Amendment?
choix: The vote of Congress, which adopts the abolitionist text by a wider majority
Ratification by three-quarters of the states, which only the 1865 text obtains
President Lincoln's signature, which Buchanan had refused for Corwin
The chronological order of the two texts, the second automatically receiving the next number
quiz_supplementaire.explication: What the Constitution retains from a proposal depends on the three-quarters of the states that ratify it, not on the majority that votes for it: only the 1865 text reaches that threshold, thanks to Georgia on December 6, 1865.
